newsitem.title: USA: Treasury aims to sell more U.S. Savings Bonds.
newsitem.headline: Treasury aims to sell more U.S. Savings Bonds.

text.p: The Treasury Department Wednesday announced it will sell $29 billion of new securities next week to help pay for government operations during the second quarter and said it was trying to make U.S. Savings Bonds more attractive for investors.

With tax receipts pouring into its coffers, the Treasury said it will pay down the government's debt by a record $65 billion during the April-June second quarter -- an unusual occurrence made possible by a booming economy that has fattened incomes.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, speaking at a press conference where details of the next week's regular quarterly refunding sales were issued, used the occasion to laud the Clinton administration's management of the economy.
"I think this announcement demonstrates that we have been responsible and conservative in our budget forecasting and suggests that the deficit will be down for a fifth year in a row," Rubin said.

Last year, the government had a deficit on its spending of $107 billion. The quarterly refunding auctions run by the Treasury generally must raise money to cover the overall shortfall between the government's spending and its income.

In the second quarter, though, the Treasury has enough coming in because individual tax payments were so high leading up to the April 15 filing deadline for 1996 returns that it can pay down debt instead of increase its borrowing.
Rubin said U.S. savings rates were "far too low" and needed to be raised. To help achieve that, he said the Treasury was taking steps to boost the return for investors who buy U.S Savings Bonds.
The changes, to take effect on Thursday, include paying interest on the bonds monthly instead of every six months and changing the way in which interest rates are calculated.

Rather than using a combination of short- and long-term market interest rates to set the yield on the bonds, the Treasury will use only long-term rates. It also will raise the percentage of market rates that will be paid on the bonds to 90 percent from 85 percent.
The moves will raise the yield on Savings Bond holdings by about 1 percentage point in the first five years of ownership and by about one quarter percentage point for later years.

Sales of U.S. Savings Bonds have fallen steadily, partly because of past Treasury actions that lowered their effective yield. Sales in the 1996 fiscal year ended last Sept. 30 were down to $6 billion from $7.2 billion in 1995 and from $9.5 billion in 1994.
Sales had reached $17.5 billion in fiscal 1993, but then the Treasury cut the minimum guranteed return on U.S. Savings Bonds to 4 percent from 6 percent and a sales slide set in.
The refunding auctions by the Treasury next week consist of a $17 billion sale of three-year notes next Tuesday and $12 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday.

After taking into account these auctions along with its regular weekly sales of 3- and six-month bills, 52-week bills and two- and five-year notes, the Treasury anticipates having a $35 billion cash balance on June 30 after paying down $65 billion of debt.
The paydown will be short-lived, however.

During the July-August third quarter, the Treasury will resume large-scale borrowing to finance the government's debts. It estimated it will borrow between $40 billion and $45 billion in the third quarter by selling Treasury securities to investors.
